Wet H2S damage in plain terms: four forms, one source of hydrogen

Short answer: In wet H2S service, corrosion of carbon steel releases atomic hydrogen at the steel surface. Dissolved H2S stops much of that hydrogen from combining into gas, so it enters the steel instead. What the hydrogen does next decides which of four damage forms develops. It can collect at inclusions and laminations and cause blistering or hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC). It can stack up under weld residual stress as stress-oriented HIC (SOHIC). Or it can crack hard microstructures directly as sulfide stress cracking (SSC). Each form needs a different NDE approach.

API RP 571 (third edition, 2020) groups these four forms under wet H2S damage for refinery equipment, mostly carbon and low-alloy steels. The forms share a single environmental cause, but their metallurgy and stress drivers differ, and so does where in the component you have to look.

  • Hydrogen blistering. Hydrogen atoms diffuse to voids, laminations or non-metallic inclusions, especially elongated manganese sulfide stringers in older, "dirtier" plate. There they combine into molecular hydrogen, which cannot diffuse out. Pressure builds until the metal bulges into a blister, usually on the process side. Blistering does not need applied stress.
  • Hydrogen-induced cracking (HIC). When the trapped hydrogen sits at inclusions or laminations at different depths in the wall, the small blister-type cracks link up through the thickness in a stepwise pattern. This is why HIC is also called stepwise cracking. HIC is mainly a plate-quality problem and does not need external stress.
  • Stress-oriented HIC (SOHIC). SOHIC is an array of small HIC-type cracks stacked on top of each other and aligned through the thickness by high tensile stress. The stress is usually weld residual stress in the heat-affected zone of welds that have not been stress relieved. SOHIC can start from existing HIC or from SSC at a weld toe. It is often the most dangerous form because it runs through-wall near welds.
  • Sulfide stress cracking (SSC). SSC is a form of hydrogen embrittlement of high-strength or hard microstructures, such as hard weld metal, hard heat-affected zones and high-strength bolting, under tensile stress. It can be fast and gives little warning.

The upstream sour-service standard most readers know is NACE MR0175/ISO 15156, which governs material selection for oil and gas production. For refinery equipment the equivalent materials document is NACE MR0103/ISO 17945. Inspection, repair and mitigation of existing refinery equipment in wet H2S service is addressed by AMPP (formerly NACE) SP0296. Use the right family of documents for your asset. See our MR0175 overview and MR0103 overview.

Where wet H2S damage turns up in refineries and gas plants

Wet H2S damage needs free water with dissolved H2S in contact with the steel. Equipment that only carries dry sour gas is generally not at risk. The usual hot spots in North American refineries and gas processing plants are the following:

  • Sour water strippers and sour water piping.
  • FCC main fractionator overhead systems and the gas plant (absorbers, strippers, accumulators).
  • Amine regenerator overheads, reflux systems, and rich-amine equipment where free water is present.
  • Hydroprocessing reactor effluent trains downstream of water injection.
  • Flare knock-out drums, compressor interstage drums, and sour gas separators in gas plants.
  • Coker fractionator overheads and gas plants.

API RP 571 lists the factors that make the environment more severe: higher H2S content in the water, pH away from neutral (both acidic conditions and alkaline sour water with cyanides increase hydrogen charging), and the presence of cyanides or other species that keep the corroding surface active. Steel factors include inclusion content and shape (which drive HIC and blistering), hardness (which drives SSC), and whether welds were post-weld heat treated (which drives SOHIC). Exact severity thresholds belong to the licensed RP 571 and owner specifications. Confirm them there rather than from secondary summaries.

A note on the summary above this section: wet H2S damage is a cracking and blistering mechanism. Wall-thickness surveys do not show it. Thickness surveys are still needed for the general corrosion that comes with it, but a CML programme on its own is not a wet H2S inspection programme.

Form-by-form: which NDE finds what

This is the table most sour-service inspection plans need. Each damage form sits in a different location, so the method has to match the form.

Damage formWhere it sitsPrimary NDESupporting / sizingNotes
Hydrogen blisteringMid-wall laminations, bulging toward the process sideVisual during internal entry (bulges); straight-beam UTUT C-scan / corrosion mapping to map extent and depthBlisters near welds or with cracking at their edges need closer attention
HIC (stepwise)Parallel to plate surface at inclusion planes; links through thicknessStraight-beam and angle-beam UT, automated UT or PAUT mappingTOFD or PAUT for through-wall linkageOften mistaken for laminations; trend the indications over time
SOHICWeld heat-affected zones and high-stress areas, through-wall stackingPAUT and TOFD from the outside; shear-wave UTWFMT on the ID to find surface-breaking initiationMost critical form; requires sizing of through-wall extent
SSCHard weld metal and HAZ, hard spots, high-strength boltingWet fluorescent magnetic particle testing (WFMT) on prepared surfacesShear-wave UT / PAUT for depth; portable hardness testingHardness data is part of the evaluation, not an optional extra

A few practical points decide the results:

  • WFMT needs real surface preparation. Wet H2S cracks are tight. They are often filled with iron sulfide scale and invisible under scale or coating. Industry practice is to clean welds and heat-affected zones by abrasive blasting or grinding to bright metal before fluorescent MT. A wire-brush clean misses cracks. The prep scope (which welds, what width either side) should be defined before the shutdown, because it drives schedule and labour more than the examination does.
  • Radiography is not the method for HIC or SOHIC. These cracks lie parallel to the surface or as tight stacks, so they give little film contrast. RT may show a large blister or an open crack, but it should not be listed as the detection method for these forms.
  • UT technique matters. HIC shows up as mid-wall reflectors that can look like plate laminations. The difference is that HIC indications change over time and usually sit in sour-service plate with active charging. A baseline UT mapping survey, repeated at the next inspection, is the most reliable way to tell growing HIC from stable manufacturing laminations.
  • External screening is possible but limited. Where internal entry is not practical, PAUT and TOFD from the outside can find and size HIC and SOHIC in the wall and near welds. Surface-breaking ID cracks at weld toes are best confirmed with WFMT from inside.

Method pages: phased array inspection, TOFD testing, magnetic particle testing in refining and corrosion mapping.

Hardness, PWHT and HIC-resistant steel: the materials controls an inspector checks

Inspection finds damage. Materials controls are what stop it from forming. When reviewing a sour-service vessel, the inspector usually checks the following records.

  • Weld hardness. For SSC in refinery carbon steel weldments, NACE SP0472 sets the long-standing refining practice of a maximum 200 HBW on production weld deposits. The value is deliberately below the HRC 22 often quoted in upstream sour-service rules, to allow for weld variability and portable-tester scatter. Check the current SP0472 and owner specifications for HAZ requirements and test methods.
  • Post-weld heat treatment. PWHT lowers residual stress and hardness, which reduces both SSC and SOHIC susceptibility. Repairs on sour-service equipment that skip PWHT, or that use alternative methods without engineering review, are a recurring source of new cracking.
  • HIC-resistant plate. Modern sour-service plate is often supplied as HIC-tested steel: low sulfur, inclusion shape control, and tested to NACE TM0284. TM0284 is a laboratory test of HIC (stepwise cracking) resistance. It does not test SSC resistance, so HIC-tested plate still needs hardness control at welds.
  • Coatings, cladding and process changes. Stainless or alloy cladding, coatings, water-wash and polysulfide or inhibitor injection are mitigation choices made by the owner. Inspection should confirm that cladding is intact and that coatings have not failed.

Older vessels built from conventional plate before HIC-resistant steels were common, and without PWHT, generally carry higher susceptibility. A good inspection plan sets its scope from that history and not from the age of the vessel alone.

Building the inspection plan: what goes into a wet H2S scope

Under API 510 for vessels and API 570 for piping, the owner's inspection plan has to address every credible damage mechanism. For wet H2S service a defensible plan usually covers these points:

  • Susceptibility screening per item. Water present, H2S level, pH and cyanides, material and plate type, PWHT status, hardness records and repair history. The owner's mechanism review or integrity engineers assign susceptibility. Where the owner runs an API 580/581 risk-based programme, that analysis sets priority and interval. Risk-based inspection is an engineering service the owner commissions. It is separate from the NDE work.
  • Weld coverage. Which welds (longitudinal, circumferential, nozzle, attachment, repair) get WFMT and what percentage. Weld coverage is often expanded when any cracking is found.
  • Volumetric mapping. Baseline UT or PAUT mapping of shell plates and heads for HIC and blistering, repeated at a set frequency so changes can be trended.
  • External in-service screening. PAUT/TOFD between internal inspections on high-susceptibility items. Results go to the inspector.
  • Hardness surveys on repairs and on welds whose records are missing.
  • Disposition path. If cracking or blistering is found, the owner decides on removal by grinding, repair with qualified procedures and PWHT, replacement, or an engineering fitness-for-service assessment. API 579-1/ASME FFS-1 has a dedicated part for hydrogen blisters, HIC and SOHIC. That assessment is commissioned by the owner from qualified engineers, and Atlantis does not perform it.

Inspection intervals for vessels in this service are discussed separately in our article on API 510 inspection intervals in sour and wet H2S service. The short version: API 510 sets no special sour-service interval. The owner's programme and damage-mechanism assessment drive the frequency within the code's general rules.

Worked example (qualitative): an FCC gas plant absorber

An older carbon steel absorber in an FCC gas plant handles wet sour gas with some cyanide. The vessel was not post-weld heat treated, and plate records show conventional (not HIC-tested) steel. During the turnaround, all internal welds and HAZs are blast-cleaned and examined with WFMT. Several transverse indications are found at a nozzle weld toe, and hardness readings there come out above the owner's limit. PAUT from outside sizes the indications as shallow surface cracks with some HIC stacking near the toe, which is the SOHIC pattern. A UT mapping baseline of the shell finds scattered mid-wall indications away from welds that have not changed since the previous survey, and they are classed as laminations to monitor.

The owner's API 510 inspector reviews the data. Engineering decides to grind out the cracks, repair with a qualified procedure, apply PWHT, and add the vessel to an external PAUT screening programme between turnarounds. The mid-wall indications become trending locations. Every decision in this example belongs to the owner and the inspector. The NDE provides measured, located evidence for each one.

Common mistakes in sour-service inspection files

  • Listing "UT thickness" as the wet H2S method. Thickness does not detect HIC, SOHIC or SSC.
  • Dry MT or visible MT on uncleaned welds. Fine SSC and SOHIC initiation needs fluorescent wet MT on properly prepared surfaces.
  • Treating every mid-wall UT indication as HIC, or every one as a lamination. Without a baseline and trending you cannot tell them apart.
  • Repairs without hardness and PWHT verification. These reintroduce the conditions that cause SSC and SOHIC.
  • Using upstream documents for refinery equipment. That means MR0175/ISO 15156 where MR0103/ISO 17945 and SP0296 apply, or the reverse.
  • Old clause references. API RP 571 was reorganised in its 2020 third edition. Plans that cite second-edition section numbers should be updated.

Regulatory overlay in the US and Canada

Wet H2S damage management sits inside the mechanical-integrity programme:

  • OSHA PSM (29 CFR 1910.119(j)). Covered processes need inspection and testing that follow recognised and generally accepted good engineering practice. API 510, API 570, API RP 571 and AMPP SP0296 are the usual references.
  • EPA Risk Management Program (40 CFR 68). Applies a parallel mechanical-integrity duty to many of the same facilities.
  • State boiler and pressure-vessel jurisdictions. These may also apply to some vessels.
  • Canada. Provincial pressure-equipment regulators (for example ABSA in Alberta under its integrity-management requirements, and TSSA in Ontario) oversee owner programmes, and upstream sour facilities face provincial energy-regulator rules as well.

Confirm the requirements with your jurisdiction.

How Atlantis supports wet H2S inspection

Atlantis NDT performs the NDE that wet H2S inspection plans specify, on equipment the owner identifies. ASNT-certified technicians under ASNT Level III oversight carry out WFMT on prepared welds, PAUT and TOFD for HIC and SOHIC detection and sizing, UT and corrosion mapping baselines for blistering and HIC trending, and portable hardness checks where the scope includes them. The Level III selects techniques and writes procedures. Results are reported by location and size so the owner's API 510/570 inspector can evaluate them. Atlantis is not the inspector of record. It does not perform RBI or fitness-for-service assessments, and it does not approve repairs. See pressure vessel inspection services and API 510 inspection support. More questions on HIC, SOHIC and SSC

What is the difference between HIC, SOHIC and SSC?

HIC is stepwise cracking at inclusions in the plate and needs no stress. SOHIC is HIC-type cracking stacked through the wall by high tensile stress, usually near welds that were not post-weld heat treated. SSC is hydrogen embrittlement cracking of hard microstructures under stress, such as hard welds and HAZ.

Which NDT method detects wet H2S cracking?

WFMT on blast-cleaned welds and HAZ is the main method for surface-breaking cracks. PAUT, TOFD and angle-beam UT detect and size embedded HIC and SOHIC. UT mapping tracks blistering and HIC across plates.

Can radiography detect HIC?

Not reliably. HIC lies roughly parallel to the surface and gives little radiographic contrast. Use UT-based methods.

What hardness limit applies to refinery welds in wet H2S service?

Refining practice under NACE SP0472 limits carbon steel production weld deposits to a maximum of 200 HBW. Check the current edition and your owner specification for HAZ and test-method details.

Does PWHT prevent wet H2S cracking?

PWHT reduces residual stress and hardness, which lowers SSC and SOHIC susceptibility. It does not prevent blistering or HIC, which depend on steel cleanliness and hydrogen charging.

What is NACE TM0284 used for?

It is a laboratory test that evaluates plate or pipe resistance to hydrogen-induced (stepwise) cracking. It does not test SSC resistance.

Talk to a Level III about WFMT and PAUT for your next turnaround or ask for a quote on sour-service vessel NDE.
